title: How Do 2FA Codes Actually Work?
sources: IETF RFC 6238 'TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm' (May 2011): TOTP = HOTP(K, T) where K is a shared secret and T = (current Unix time - T0) / X; 'default value X = 30 seconds'
IETF RFC 4226 / RFC 6238 section 1.2: HOTP(K,C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA-1(K,C)), truncated to a short decimal code (6 digits is common)
IETF RFC 6238 section 5.2: the validator computes the same value; 'We RECOMMEND that at most one time step is allowed as the network delay'

Google Account Help, 'Get verification codes with Google Authenticator' (support.google.com/accounts/answer/1066447): 'You can still generate codes without an internet connection or mobile service'; setup is done by scanning a QR code that carries the secret key

lines.text: Those six-digit login codes that change every thirty seconds,
where do they actually come from?
You'd think a server texts them to you,
but nothing is sent at all.
When you scanned that QR code during setup,
your phone and the website saved the same secret.
your app mixes that secret with the current time
The website does the same math,
so if both numbers match, you're in.
it works even in airplane mode,
because the code is made right on your phone.
lines.caps: BECAUSE THE *CODE | IS *MADE | RIGHT ON YOUR *PHONE

lines.text: Your phone and the website never talk, they just both check the clock.
lines.caps: YOUR *PHONE | AND THE *WEBSITE | *NEVER TALK | THEY JUST *BOTH | CHECK THE *CLOCK
